name: Tampuan
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.

tone_statements.citation: Huffman, Franklin E. 1976. The register problem in fifteen Mon-Khmer languages. In Philip N. Jenner, Laurence C. Thompson & Stanley Starosta (eds.), Austroasiatic Studies, Part I (Oceanic Linguistics Special Publication 13), 575-589. Honolulu: University Press of Hawaii.
tone_statements.quote: While Tampuon and Mal can also be analyzed in terms of two contrasting series of initial stops corresponding to original */p t c k/ and */b d j g/, they show somewhat separate development. Tampuon has what might be called the standard inventory of initials … completely reduplicated by a set of initials characterized by post-glottalization in the case of stops and simultaneous glottalization in the case [of] the continuants. Oddly, however, it is glottalized [ini]tials which condition breathy vowel allophones … in any case register is clearly sub[pho]nemic in this language.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 581-582, paragraph on Tampuon in the language survey

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: Coding fixed-dominant, rule 01 (main-syllable-final prominence in sesquisyllabic words) rests on Crowley 2000, the sole phonological description of Tampuan in Glottolog and on the web. The PDF was not yet obtained; it is now and the deciding quotation is confirmed verbatim on p. 2 (p. 3 reinforces it). Nothing better exists to judge against, and the statement is the uncontroversial Bahnaric sesquisyllabic pattern, so the record is well-sourced; the only action is to fill the empty grade/cite/loc fields (cite Crowley 2000 MKS 30, p. 2; copies we hold path above) rather than any reclassify. list of works to obtain is a single low-priority print dictionary.

sources.citation: Crowley 2000, Tampuan phonology, Mon-Khmer Studies 30, pp. 2-3 (sealang.net PDF, pages re-read)
sources.quote: the phonological word (PW) is composed of a main (tonic) syllable optionally preceded by a pre- (atonic) syllable ... The presyllable C(R)V(N)- characterizes a range of possible weakly stressed syllables

sources.citation: Crowley, James Dale. 2000. Tampuan phonology. Mon-Khmer Studies 30: 1-21.
sources.quote: PW = C(R)V(N)-C(C)V(C): 'a main (tonic) syllable optionally preceded by a pre- (atonic) syllable'; presyllable vowel 'unstressed'; presyllables are 'weakly stressed syllables'; nasal presyllables 'still maintain a separate weak stress' (p. 3). I.e. prominence on the final (main) syllable of every disyllable = rule 01.

sources.citation: Huffman, Franklin E. 1976. The register problem in fifteen Mon-Khmer languages. In Philip N. Jenner, Laurence C. Thompson & Stanley Starosta (eds.), Austroasiatic Studies, Part I (Oceanic Linguistics Special Publication 13), 575-589. Honolulu: University Press of Hawaii.
sources.quote: While Tampuon and Mal can also be analyzed in terms of two contrasting series of initial stops corresponding to original */p t c k/ and */b d j g/, they show somewhat separate development. Tampuon has what might be called the standard inventory of initials … completely reduplicated by a set of initials characterized by post-glottalization in the case of stops and simultaneous glottalization in the case [of] the continuants. Oddly, however, it is glottalized [ini]tials which condition breathy vowel allophones … in any case register is clearly sub[pho]nemic in this language.
sources.locator: pp. 581-582, paragraph on Tampuon in the language survey
sources.note: No tone is described. Huffman finds Tampuon's breathy vs clear vowel register only allophonic (after glottalized initials), i.e. sub-phonemic; Crowley 2000 treats register as phonation, not pitch.
